name: Glasses frame selection by face shape

lead: This is choosing frame shapes that balance or complement your face, sometimes to add a more angular look or a hunter-eyes impression.

Frame lines, colour and size are said to contrast or echo your features and shift where the eye is drawn. Pairing rules by face shape are widely repeated in styling advice; no studies testing them were found.

paras: People try several shapes in a shop or with virtual try-on, comparing frames with their jaw, brow and cheekbone lines, and often ask for opinions or photos. The frames change the look as soon as they are worn.
No health risks. Poorly fitting frames can be uncomfortable, and the effect on appearance is subjective.

web.title: WebMD: How to pick the right glasses for your face shape

angle.text: Choosing frame shapes that balance or complement your face changes how your features read once the glasses are on, and some users aim for a hunter-eyes look. The pairing rules are widely repeated styling advice rather than tested findings.

lead: Glasses frame selection by face shape is a style practice of choosing frames whose shape and size balance or flatter the wearer's face. The common principle in eyewear guides is contrast: angular frames to soften a round face, rounder frames to soften a square jaw, with frame width and position used to bring attention to the eyes.[1][2] People in appearance communities use it as an easy styling change, and some discuss frame shape as a way to alter the perceived eye area.

The usual guidance, as given in a medically reviewed WebMD guide dated December 2024, is that round faces suit bold angular frames such as rectangular, geometric or cat-eye styles; square faces suit round or oval frames, with thin frames slightly wider than the cheekbones; oval faces are the most versatile; and heart-shaped faces suit aviator and D-frames that are a little wider than the forehead.[1] The same guide places frame position as a tip, for example setting frames just above the cheekbones on round faces.[1]

Glasses themselves have gone from being seen as unfashionable, associated with age and frailty, to a key part of personal image, helped by public figures such as Harold Lloyd and Buddy Holly, and designers now release seasonal eyewear collections.[3] No published study has tested whether matching frame shape to face shape changes perceived attractiveness; the face-shape rules come from optical retailers and style guides.
infobox: Aviator, browline, cat-eye, horn-rimmed, rimless, Wayfarer, round, rectangular[3]
Frame shape contrasts with face shape[1][2]
Lens width, bridge width, temple length in mm, e.g. 54-15-143[2]

paras: Frames are built from eye wires, bridge, brow bar, nose pads, temples and hinges, in plastics such as cellulose acetate, metals such as titanium and stainless steel, and natural materials.[3] Face-shape guidance sorts faces into categories such as round, square, oval, heart, triangle and diamond, and recommends frame shapes for each.[1][2]

Round: bold, angular frames, with rectangular frames making the face look longer, geometric frames adding sharp lines and cat-eye frames highlighting the eyes and cheeks.[1] Square: round or oval frames to soften strong angles, with thin frames slightly wider than the cheekbones.[1] Oval: described as the most versatile, suiting geometric, rectangular, square, oversized, cat-eye and aviator styles.[1] Heart: aviator and D-frames that shift focus from the forehead, a bit wider than the forehead, with detail at the bottom; AllAboutVision adds that circular frames suit heart-shaped faces with high cheekbones.[1][2] Triangle: bold-top frames such as cat-eye, aviator or D-frames to draw attention up from the jaw.[1]

Guides advise that many faces fall between two shapes, so frames suited to both can be tried, and frames that look right can still fit poorly.[1] Frame markings give lens width, bridge width and temple length in millimetres, and weight should match lens thickness, with sturdier frames suiting thicker lenses.[2] Higher-power lenses can become thick and heavy in large shapes, rounded frames suit nearsighted prescriptions well, and high-index lenses are lighter and thinner.[3]

Appearance communities discuss frame shape as a way to alter the perceived eye area or balance jaw and face width, treating glasses as a reversible, low-cost accessory that sits alongside haircut and grooming choices.

timeline.event: Glasses still described as 'medical appliances'; fashionable options appear from the 1970s.[3]
WebMD publishes a medically reviewed frame-by-face-shape guide (6 December).[1]
